item.title: The Fighting Temeraire
item.lesson: The HMS Temeraire fought heroically at Trafalgar in 1805, second in line behind Nelson's Victory. Thirty-three years later she was sold for scrap and towed up the Thames to be broken apart — and Turner turned the news item into an elegy for an entire age. The old warship glides ghost-pale and rigged like a cathedral, pulled by a squat black steam tug, fire in its stack: sail and steam, past and future, in one procession. Behind them Turner stages the most famous sunset in British art, a furnace of paint that no sky ever quite produced — he moved the sun, invented the colors, and put masts back on a ship that had already been stripped. Every literal fact is wrong; the truth is exact. Turner called it his 'darling' and refused every offer to sell, leaving it to the British nation at his death. In 2005, BBC listeners voted it the greatest painting in Britain, and it now sails on the back of the twenty-pound note.
item.lookFor: Compare the two vessels' colors: the Temeraire painted in whites and golds like a ghost already, the tug in blacks and rust — and note it is the little tug, not the sunset, that owns the picture's only urgent energy.
